additions.reason: Levi is the origin of melody in the world. The Zohar (Shemot p.19) cited in the Torah states that the main melody comes from the sitra of Levi. Levi's bechina IS melody — they share the same essential nature of musical/vocal attachment.

Melody and musical instruments are the bechina through which Levi brought joining/union into the world. This is the dominant concept of the Torah — it is explicitly called a 'bechina' and is the axis around which all other concepts in this Torah revolve.
additions.source_quote: עַל יָדוֹ בָּא בְּחִינַת הַנִּגּוּן וּכְלֵי שִׁיר לָעוֹלָם

additions.reason: The joining/attachment of two things is explicitly equated to melody and musical instruments — 'hitḥabrut of two things is through melody and musical instruments.' This is a bechina relationship: joining IS music, music IS joining. They are two faces of the same reality.
additions.source_quote: כִּי הִתְחַבְּרוּת שְׁנֵי דְּבָרִים הוּא עַל־יְדֵי נִגּוּן וּכְלֵי שִׁיר

additions.reason: Wedding instruments are explicitly stated to be the bechina of the above (the joining through music). The wedding context is where the hitḥabrut principle is most visibly enacted — two people are joined, and the music is the vehicle and expression of that joining.
additions.source_quote: וְזֶה בְּחִינַת כְּלֵי זֶמֶר שֶׁמְּנַגְּנִין עַל חֲתֻנָּה

additions.reason: A wedding (ḥatunah) is the archetypal joining of two people into one. In the Torah's framework, a wedding is the concrete instantiation of hitḥabrut — the very event that the music facilitates. The bechina of wedding music (kele zemer she-menagnim al ḥatunah) implies the wedding itself as a member of this cluster.

All five nodes above are new additions derived from the source text. The Torah uses explicit bechina language three times: (1) 'בָּא בְּחִינַת הַנִּגּוּן' connecting melody to Levi, (2) 'הִתְחַבְּרוּת... הוּא עַל יְדֵי נִגּוּן' equating joining to music, and (3) 'וְזֶה בְּחִינַת כְּלֵי זֶמֶר שֶׁמְּנַגְּנִין עַל חֲתֻנָּה' applying the bechina to the wedding context. Note also the wordplay the Rebbe draws on: the root ל-ו-ה means both the name Levi, the word for 'attachment/joining' (יִלָּוֶה), and musical 'accompaniment' — all three meanings collapse into each other as an expression of the bechina relationship. The third line (rachash wordplay) is editorial and does not contain bechina edges.
